title: I Ranked Cloudflare’s Software Factory and Wow… S TIER TOKENOMICS
summary: Dan breaks down Cloudflare's AI code review software factory from a blog post by Ryan Skidmore: in one month, 130,000 AI reviews across 5,000 codebases at a median cost of $1 per merge request, powered by a CI-native orchestration system built on the open-source OpenCode agent with a composable plugin architecture. He grades each element of the factory on his first agentic engineering tier list (F through S plus a legendary ZTE level). Tokenomics and system resilience earn S; agents-plus-code pipelines, the plugin-based extensible factory, context engineering, prompt engineering, agent observability (Braintrust), and model flexibility earn A; the simple coordinator-plus-specialists orchestration, agent specialization, and harness engineering get B; a single custom tool, human-out-of-the-loop, and always-on get C; and self-improving systems get F. He closes with the ZTE mindset - zero-touch engineering as phase three beyond building trust with agents - and a final grade of A for Cloudflare's agentic engineering.
what_you_learn: You learn the concrete anatomy of a production-grade multi-agent code review system: CI-triggered orchestration with up to seven specialized reviewer agents fused by a coordinator, JSONL streaming for real-time observability, risk-tiered compute scaling, model fallbacks, and escape hatches like the break-glass comment. It is a blueprint for designing your own agent harness instead of renting a closed one.

skills.name: Token Economics
skills.description: Using tokens to generate value and arbitraging that value for more than it cost - Cloudflare hit $1 per AI code review.

skills.name: Agent Harness Engineering
skills.description: Owning and customizing your open-source agent harness (OpenCode) instead of renting a closed coding tool.

skills.name: Code Review
skills.description: Splitting review across up to seven domain-specific agents (security, performance, code quality, documentation, release management, compliance) instead of one generalist.

skills.name: Multi-Agent Orchestration
skills.description: A coordinator agent that dedupes, recategorizes, verifies, and fuses specialist findings into one structured review comment.

skills.name: Agent Observability
skills.description: Agents writing structured output as JSONL so every streamed line is valid, enabling real-time event triggers like step-finish.

skills.name: Agent Guardrails
skills.description: Scaling the number of deployed agents to the size and risk of the diff - two agents for trivial changes, all seven for large ones.

skills.name: Model Selection & Routing
skills.description: A three-tier model stack (state-of-the-art, workhorse, lightweight) with provider fallback so the system never goes down.

skills.name: Software Architecture
skills.description: Retry logic, error classification, model and provider fallbacks, and incremental re-reviews that carry prior context.

skills.name: Software Factory
skills.description: The phase-three north star of shipping from a single prompt with humans out of the loop.

learnings.title: The headline numbers: 130,000 reviews at a median of $1 each
learnings.detail: Cloudflare ran 130,000 AI code reviews across 5,000 repositories in a single month at a median cost of $1 per merge request, consuming 120 billion tokens, with reviews completing in about 3 minutes. The agents found roughly 8,000 critical issues - the code quality agent alone found 6,000 and security found over 400. Dan calls this a massive token arbitrage and gives Cloudflare an S tier in tokenomics, the skill of spending tokens to generate value worth more than the spend.

learnings.title: The problem: code review is the bottleneck constraint
learnings.detail: In the age of agents there are two constraints - planning and reviewing - and Cloudflare attacks reviewing. The classic loop (MR queued, reviewer context-switches, nitpicks, back-and-forth, merge) has a median first-review wait measured in hours, and the author loses context every second they wait. With AI review the engineering owner gets feedback within minutes and a human reviewer can then review the comments rather than the raw diff, hard-blocking or approving much faster.

learnings.title: Why they built a custom harness on OpenCode instead of using off-the-shelf tools
learnings.detail: Cloudflare first tried existing AI coding tools, but none offered enough flexibility and customization for an organization their size - the recurring theme that custom solutions are specialized by nature. They then tried naive vibe coding (shoving the diff into a half-baked prompt), which produced noise, hallucinated syntax, and useless advice. So they built a CI-native orchestration system on OpenCode, chosen because they already used it internally, it is open source so they can contribute upstream, and its SDK enables programmatic agent sessions - a prerequisite for any legitimate agentic coding tool.

learnings.title: Architecture: CI trigger, coordinator agent, and up to seven specialists
learnings.detail: A GitLab merge request triggers CI, which loads the orchestration system. A coordinator agent (the orchestrator) calls a single custom tool, spawn_reviewers, which kicks off up to seven specialized sub-agents covering security, performance, code quality, documentation, release management, and compliance with the internal engineering codex. Sub-agents return structured XML findings with severity classifications; the coordinator fuses them via a fusion prompt into one comment. Dan ranks the orchestration itself only B - a simple delegation pattern - because the real value is the specialization, not the novelty.

learnings.title: Plugin architecture: agents plus code with a three-phase lifecycle
learnings.detail: The system is built on a composable plugin architecture where an entry point delegates all configuration to plugins that compose together to define how a review runs. Each plugin implements a review-plugin interface with three lifecycle hooks: bootstrap, configure, and post-configure (which runs after the configuration is assembled). A JSON config file loads everything into the harness. Dan gives this agents-plus-code approach an A: deterministic code manages the non-deterministic agents, and the plugin system gives 5,000 codebases extensibility and adaptability.

learnings.title: JSONL streaming is the key to real-time agent observability
learnings.detail: Sub-agents write their outputs in JSONL instead of JSON or YAML. Because every appended line is independently valid, the file is always readable and streamable while agents emit it - with plain JSON you must wait for the closing bracket and risk a truncated file if the agent errors. Cloudflare acts on stream triggers like step-finish for live tracking of costs, error detection, and retry logic (a step-finish with reason length means max tokens hit mid-sentence, so retry). Combined with Braintrust for distributed tracing, this earns agent observability an A: if you do not measure your agents, you cannot improve them.

learnings.title: Prompt engineering: tell agents what to ignore, not just what to find
learnings.detail: Each reviewer has a tightly scoped prompt defining its purpose, what to look for, and - unusually - what to ignore. Telling agents not to nitpick syntax or non-functional style and to focus on runtime behavior and security is a prompt engineering technique Dan admits he underuses. Findings come back as structured XML with a severity classification, which feeds directly into the coordinator's fusion and filtering step.

learnings.title: Context engineering: shared context files and domain-scoped diffs save 7x tokens
learnings.detail: Diffs are written to file paths rather than pasted into prompts, and each sub-reviewer reads only the patch relevant to its domain, sharing a common context file. Duplicating the full MR context across seven reviewers would multiply token cost roughly 7x. They also strip large loud files like bun.lock so no agent accidentally reads them and blows up the cost curve. This earns an A for context engineering, though cross-system architectural awareness keeps it from S.

learnings.title: Risk tiers: do not send the dream team to review a typo fix
learnings.detail: Compute spend scales with diff size and risk. Trivial changes (under 10 lines, under 20 files) get only the coordinator plus one generalist reviewer; light changes (under 100 lines, under 20 files) get about four agents; large changes (over 100 lines or 50 files) deploy the full seven-specialist pipeline. This right-sizing of compute is what makes the S-tier tokenomics possible.

learnings.title: Resilience: retries, error classification, model fallback, and provider switching
learnings.detail: The system has per-task and overall retry budgets, classifies errors to decide whether a model fallback will help, falls back to previous model versions on failures, and runs a CI job that can fetch model configuration to switch providers (Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter) when one has a bad day. Re-reviews are incremental: the coordinator receives the full context of the previous review instead of starting from scratch. This earns system resilience an S.

learnings.title: Human escape hatches: bias toward approval with a break-glass override
learnings.detail: The final decision rubric is explicitly biased toward approval: a warning in an otherwise clean MR is approved with comments rather than blocked. If a human reviewer comments 'break glass', the system forces approval regardless of what the AI found - the AI can hard-block merges on genuine security issues, but humans are never limited by it. Even so, Dan ranks human-out-of-the-loop a C (dropped from B) because the system still yells at engineers to update agents.md, and self-improving systems an F because agents.md rots quickly and nothing updates it automatically.

learnings.title: The verdict: A overall, and ZTE as the phase-three north star
learnings.detail: Final tier list: tokenomics S, system resilience S, agents-plus-code pipeline A, extensible factory A, context engineering A, agent observability A, model flexibility A, prompt engineering A, multi-agent orchestration and agent specialization B, custom tools C, human out of the loop C, always on C, spend to learn C, self-improving F. ZTE - zero-touch engineering - stays empty: phase one is prompting back and forth, phase two is building trust and scaling compute, phase three is prompt-to-production. He advises job seekers to avoid any company that is not AI-first.

key_points: Cloudflare ran 130,000 AI code reviews across 5,000 repos for a median of $1 per merge request - reviews land in about 3 minutes.
The agent team found about 8,000 critical issues; the code quality specialist alone found 6,000.
Seven specialized reviewer agents beat one generalist with a massive prompt - and the coordinator fuses their findings into one comment.
JSONL output means the file is always valid and streamable - real-time observability and retries without waiting for a closing JSON bracket.
Tell your agents what to ignore: scoped prompts that ban syntax nitpicks keep reviews focused on runtime, security, and real bugs.
Shared context files and domain-scoped diffs avoid a 7x token multiplication across reviewers.
Risk-tiered compute: two agents for a typo fix, four for a light change, the full seven for big diffs.
Break-glass comments force approval regardless of AI findings - humans are never hard-blocked by their own system.
Tokenomics and system resilience are S tier; self-improving systems are F - nobody is doing zero-touch engineering yet.
